Let $H$ be a Hopf algebra over a field $k$ as in [[def-hh-hopf-algebra-and-antipode]], with multiplication, unit $1$, counit $\varepsilon$, and antipode. The **left-integral space** and **right-integral space** of $H$ are
$$
\int_H^\ell=\{\Lambda\in H:h\Lambda=\varepsilon(h)\Lambda\text{ for every }h\in H\},\qquad
\int_H^r=\{\Lambda\in H:\Lambda h=\varepsilon(h)\Lambda\text{ for every }h\in H\}.
$$
Both are linear subspaces and include zero. When $H$ is finite-dimensional, its dual $H^*$ is a Hopf algebra. Its product is convolution $(f*g)(h)=\sum f(h_1)g(h_2)$ and its counit is $\varepsilon_{H^*}(f)=f(1)$. A **left integral functional** on $H$ means an element $\lambda\in H^*$ satisfying $f*\lambda=f(1)\lambda$ for every $f\in H^*$; a **right integral functional** satisfies $\lambda*f=f(1)\lambda$. Zero is allowed in both definitions; existence of a nonzero integral is a theorem, not part of the definition.

Let $k$ be a field, $H$ a Hopf algebra over $k$, and $M$ a $k$-vector space. A **right $H$-module structure** on $M$ is a bilinear map $(m,h)\mapsto mh$ satisfying $(mh)g=m(hg)$ and $m1_H=m$. A **right $H$-comodule structure** is a linear map $\rho:M\to M\otimes H$ satisfying
$$
(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id}_H)\rho=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\Delta)\rho,\qquad (\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho=\operatorname{id}_M.
$$
Write $\rho(m)=\sum m_0\otimes m_1$ and $\Delta(h)=\sum h_1\otimes h_2$, where each expression denotes a finite tensor sum. The pair of structures makes $M$ a **right-right Hopf module** if it satisfies
$$
\rho(mh)=\sum m_0h_1\otimes m_1h_2\qquad(m\in M,\ h\in H).
$$
A **morphism of right-right Hopf modules** is a linear map preserving both the right action and right coaction. The **coinvariants** are the subset
$$
M^{\operatorname{co}H}:=\{m\in M:\rho(m)=m\otimes1_H\}.
$$
The next lemma proves that this subset is a $k$-subspace. No finite-dimensionality of $H$ or $M$, and no bijectivity of the antipode, is part of the definition.

Let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces.

1. The bilinear map $V^*\times W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$, $(f,g)\mapsto[v\otimes w\mapsto f(v)g(w)]$, induces an isomorphism $V^*\otimes W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$. For ordered bases $(v_1,\dots,v_m)$ of $V$, $(w_1,\dots,w_n)$ of $W$ with dual bases $(v_i^*)$, $(w_j^*)$, the image of $v_i^*\otimes w_j^*$ is the dual basis vector of $v_i\otimes w_j$ in the product basis of $V\otimes W$.
2. For every ordered basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $V$ the element $\sum_{i=1}^nv_i^*\otimes v_i\in V^*\otimes V$ is independent of the basis and corresponds to $\mathrm{id}_V$ under the isomorphism $V^*\otimes V\to\operatorname{Hom}(V,V)$, $f\otimes v\mapsto[x\mapsto f(x)v]$ ([[thm-hom-from-a-finite-dimensional-space-as-a-tensor-product]]). Its image under $\sigma_{V^*,V}$ is the corresponding element $\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$ of $V\otimes V^*$.
3. The evaluation $\mathrm{ev}:V^*\otimes V\to k$, $f\otimes v\mapsto f(v)$, and the coevaluation $\mathrm{coev}:k\to V\otimes V^*$, $1\mapsto\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$, are independent of the basis and satisfy $(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes\mathrm{ev})\circ\alpha_{V,V^*,V}\circ(\mathrm{coev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_V)=\mathrm{id}_V$ and $(\mathrm{ev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{V^*})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{V^*,V,V^*}\circ(\mathrm{id}_{V^*}\otimes\mathrm{coev})=\mathrm{id}_{V^*}$, the unit isomorphisms $k\otimes V\cong V$, $V\otimes k\cong V$ being understood.

Let $H$ be a Hopf algebra over a field $k$, with antipode $S$, multiplication $m$, unit $u$, comultiplication $\Delta$, and counit $\varepsilon$. Then $S$ is unique, $S(1)=1$, and $\varepsilon\circ S=\varepsilon$. Moreover, for all $a,b\in H$,

$$S(ab)=S(b)S(a),\qquad \Delta(S(h))=(S\otimes S)\tau\Delta(h)\quad(h\in H),$$

where $\tau(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$ is the tensor flip. In particular, these are consequences of the convolution-inverse definition; they are not extra axioms.

Let $k$ be a field and $H=(H,m,u,\Delta,\varepsilon,S)$ a finite-dimensional Hopf $k$-algebra. Give $H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(H,k)$ the transposed Hopf structure: multiplication is convolution,
$$
(\phi\psi)(h)=(\phi\otimes\psi)(\Delta(h)),
$$
the unit is $\varepsilon$, coproduct is the transpose $m^*:H^*\to H^*\otimes H^*$ under finite tensor duality, the counit is $\phi\mapsto\phi(1_H)$, and the antipode is $S^*(\phi)=\phi\circ S$. Then $H^*$ is a Hopf algebra. No bijectivity assumption on $S$ is required.

A **Hopf algebra over $k$** is a bialgebra $H$ together with a $k$-linear map $S:H\to H$, called its **antipode**, such that

$$S*\mathrm{id}_H=u\varepsilon=\mathrm{id}_H*S,$$

where $*$ is the convolution product on $\operatorname{Hom}_k(H,H)$, $u:k\to H$ is the unit, and $\varepsilon:H\to k$ is the counit. Equivalently, $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta=u\varepsilon=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta$. Thus $S$ is the two-sided inverse of $\mathrm{id}_H$ in the convolution algebra. This definition imposes no compositional bijectivity condition on $S$.

Let $H$ be a Hopf algebra over a field $k$ as in [[def-hh-hopf-algebra-and-antipode]], with multiplication, unit $1$, counit $\varepsilon$, and antipode. The **left-integral space** and **right-integral space** of $H$ are
$$
\int_H^\ell=\{\Lambda\in H:h\Lambda=\varepsilon(h)\Lambda\text{ for every }h\in H\},\qquad
\int_H^r=\{\Lambda\in H:\Lambda h=\varepsilon(h)\Lambda\text{ for every }h\in H\}.
$$
Both are linear subspaces and include zero. When $H$ is finite-dimensional, its dual $H^*$ is a Hopf algebra. Its product is convolution $(f*g)(h)=\sum f(h_1)g(h_2)$ and its counit is $\varepsilon_{H^*}(f)=f(1)$. A **left integral functional** on $H$ means an element $\lambda\in H^*$ satisfying $f*\lambda=f(1)\lambda$ for every $f\in H^*$; a **right integral functional** satisfies $\lambda*f=f(1)\lambda$. Zero is allowed in both definitions; existence of a nonzero integral is a theorem, not part of the definition.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.
A left $R$-module is **semisimple** when it is an internal direct sum of simple submodules, allowing the empty direct sum. Hence the zero module is semisimple.

A unital ring $R$ is **semisimple** when its left regular module ${}_R R$ is semisimple. This is a left-module definition and uses no Jacobson radical. For the zero ring, the regular module is zero and hence semisimple; the Wedderburn-Artin theorem below is stated for nonzero rings.

Let $k$ be a field.

1. Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ a free $R$-module of finite rank $n$ with basis $(e_0,\dots,e_{n-1})$, and let $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in M$ span $M$. Then the coordinate matrix $A$ of $(v_0,\dots,v_{n-1})$ in the basis $(e_i)$ has a right inverse, $\det(A)$ is a unit of $R$, and $(v_0,\dots,v_{n-1})$ is a basis of $M$. The determinant is formed for $n\ge1$; for $n=0$ the module is the zero module and the empty family is its basis, with no determinant clause.
2. If $F\subseteq E$ is a field extension and $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, then the rank of $A$ over $F$ equals its rank over $E$.
3. Let $B$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra and $N$ a finite-dimensional left $B$-module. A proper submodule has strictly smaller $k$-dimension, a maximal proper submodule of a nonzero finite-dimensional module exists by maximal dimension (no arbitrary Choice), and iterating produces a finite composition series of $N$ ([[def-composition-series-and-length-of-a-module]]); in particular $N$ has finite length.
4. If $S_1,\dots,S_m$ are simple $B$-modules and $N\subseteq S_1\oplus\cdots\oplus S_m$ is a submodule, then $N$ is isomorphic to a direct sum of a subfamily of the $S_i$, and $N$ has a complement in $S_1\oplus\cdots\oplus S_m$.
5. If $T:N\to N$ is $k$-linear with $T^r=0$ for some $r\ge1$, then $\operatorname{tr}(T)=0$ ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

Let $H$ be a Hopf algebra over a field $k$, with antipode $S$, multiplication $m$, unit $u$, comultiplication $\Delta$, and counit $\varepsilon$. Then $S$ is unique, $S(1)=1$, and $\varepsilon\circ S=\varepsilon$. Moreover, for all $a,b\in H$,

$$S(ab)=S(b)S(a),\qquad \Delta(S(h))=(S\otimes S)\tau\Delta(h)\quad(h\in H),$$

where $\tau(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$ is the tensor flip. In particular, these are consequences of the convolution-inverse definition; they are not extra axioms.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

Let $M$ be a left $R$-module. A subset $N\subseteq M$ is a **submodule** when
it is a subgroup of the additive group of $M$ and is closed under scalars:

$$r\in R,\ n\in N\quad\Longrightarrow\quad rn\in N.$$

The operations on $N$ are the restrictions of those of $M$. Write $N\le M$ when
the ring and module are understood.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$
If $B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)$ is a basis of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space $V$, then its dual family $B^*=(b_1^*,\ldots,b_n^*)$ is a basis of $V^*$. Consequently $\dim V^*=\dim V=n$.

citations.quote: Let $k$ be a field, $N>1$, and $\zeta\in k$ a primitive $N$-th root of unity, with $\operatorname{char}(k)\nmid N$. On the $N^2$-dimensional vector space with basis $g^i x^j$, $0\le i,j<N$, define multiplication on basis elements by $(g^i x^j)(g^a x^b)=\zeta^{-aj}g^{\,i+a\ {\rm mod}\ N}x^{j+b}$ if $j+b<N$, and by $0$ if $j+b\ge N$. Then this is an associative unital algebra and is the presented algebra $k\langle g,x\rangle/(g^N-1,\ x^N,\ gx-\zeta xg)$; the displayed basis is a basis of that quotient. It becomes a Hopf algebra with $\Delta(g)=g\otimes g$, $\Delta(x)=1\otimes x+x\otimes g$, $\varepsilon(g)=1$, $\varepsilon(x)=0$, $S(g)=g^{-1}$, and $S(x)=-xg^{-1}$.

Let $k$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital associative $k$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A bilinear form $\beta:A\times A\to k$ is **associative** when $\beta(ab,c)=\beta(a,bc)$ for all $a,b,c\in A$. It is **nondegenerate** when both linear maps
$$
A\to A^*,\qquad a\mapsto[b\mapsto\beta(a,b)],\qquad b\mapsto[a\mapsto\beta(a,b)]
$$
are isomorphisms. A linear functional $\lambda:A\to k$ is a **Frobenius functional** when $\beta_\lambda(a,b):=\lambda(ab)$ is nondegenerate. Associativity of $\beta_\lambda$ follows from associativity of multiplication. The algebra $A$ is **Frobenius** when it has at least one Frobenius functional.

Let $k$ be any field.

1. For any group $G$, the vector space $kG$ of finite sums $\sum_{g\in G}a_g g$ is a Hopf algebra. Its multiplication is the bilinear extension of the group law, its unit is the group identity $e$, and
   $$\Delta(g)=g\otimes g,\qquad \varepsilon(g)=1,\qquad S(g)=g^{-1}\quad(g\in G).$$
2. For any finite group $G$, the pointwise algebra $k^G$ of all functions $f:G\to k$ is a Hopf algebra with
   $$\Delta(f)(x,y)=f(xy),\qquad \varepsilon(f)=f(e),\qquad S(f)(x)=f(x^{-1}).$$
   The finite-set tensor identification $k^G\otimes k^G\cong k^{G\times G}$ is used to define $\Delta$. No Hopf structure on the full function space $k^G$ for infinite $G$ is claimed.
3. The polynomial algebra $k[x]$ is a Hopf algebra with
   $$\Delta(x)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x,\qquad \varepsilon(x)=0,\qquad S(x)=-x.$$
   These formulas work in every characteristic. The element $x$ is primitive in every characteristic, and in characteristic $p>0$ so is $x^p$.

Let $H$ be a Hopf algebra over a field $k$ as in [[def-hh-hopf-algebra-and-antipode]], with multiplication, unit $1$, counit $\varepsilon$, and antipode. The **left-integral space** and **right-integral space** of $H$ are
$$
\int_H^\ell=\{\Lambda\in H:h\Lambda=\varepsilon(h)\Lambda\text{ for every }h\in H\},\qquad
\int_H^r=\{\Lambda\in H:\Lambda h=\varepsilon(h)\Lambda\text{ for every }h\in H\}.
$$
Both are linear subspaces and include zero. When $H$ is finite-dimensional, its dual $H^*$ is a Hopf algebra. Its product is convolution $(f*g)(h)=\sum f(h_1)g(h_2)$ and its counit is $\varepsilon_{H^*}(f)=f(1)$. A **left integral functional** on $H$ means an element $\lambda\in H^*$ satisfying $f*\lambda=f(1)\lambda$ for every $f\in H^*$; a **right integral functional** satisfies $\lambda*f=f(1)\lambda$. Zero is allowed in both definitions; existence of a nonzero integral is a theorem, not part of the definition.

Let $H\ne0$ be a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra as in [[def-hh-hopf-algebra-and-antipode]] over a field $k$. Then $H$ is semisimple as a ring ([[def-semisimple-ring]]), that is, its left regular module is a direct sum of simple left submodules ([[def-semisimple-module]]), if and only if there exists a left integral $\Lambda\in H$ with $\varepsilon(\Lambda)\ne0$. In that case $\Lambda$ can be normalized so that $\varepsilon(\Lambda)=1$.
